title: Sudden breathlessness while jogging in a 20-year-old student
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 20-year-old law student brought to the ED by ambulance. She became suddenly short of breath an hour ago while jogging, after forgetting to take her reliever. The candidate first has to recognise how severe the attack is and start treatment. They then take a targeted history covering triggers, asthma risk and the dangerous differentials, and examine her. In Part 2 they interpret her observations, an arterial blood gas taken on oxygen and an ECG. They diagnose a severe acute asthma exacerbation, give a justified list of differentials, outline ED management under the Australian Asthma Handbook and safety-net for discharge.
focus: Acute dyspnoea in a young adult with known asthma: judging severity and starting treatment early, screening the dangerous differentials, interpreting an acute respiratory alkalosis, and managing a severe asthma exacerbation
stem: You are a final-year medical student on your Emergency Department placement at a metropolitan hospital. It is early afternoon. Sophia Bennett, a 20-year-old student, has been brought in by ambulance with shortness of breath. She is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken her observations and recorded an ECG, and the ED registrar took an arterial blood gas when she arrived. The consultant has asked you to see her.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sophia and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. She is very breathless, so keep your questions targeted (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, arterial blood gas and ECG. Give a handover with your interpretation, your diagnosis and differentials, your management and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sophia Bennett, a 20-year-old law student. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting bolt upright on the trolley, leaning forward with your hands on your knees, still in your running clothes. You are breathing fast and wheezing, and you can only say a few words at a time. You are frightened and your hands are a little shaky. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Sophia came in by ambulance about 10 minutes ago. The paramedics gave her a salbutamol neb on the way, running on 8 litres of oxygen, and she says it helped a bit. The registrar took an arterial gas on arrival while the neb was still running. On arrival her resp rate was 34, sats 98% on the neb, heart rate 130 and regular, BP 130/80. The neb finished, so I took the mask off for a room-air set just now: resp rate 32, sats 92% on room air, heart rate 126 and regular, BP 128/76, temperature 37.2. She's on the monitor, the cannula's in and the ECG is done. What would you like?"

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks, "What saturation are you aiming for?"
  • If they ask for salbutamol (puffs through a spacer or a nebuliser) with oxygen, after a few minutes you can say short sentences, the wheeze is a little quieter, sats are about 95% on oxygen and your heart rate stays about 120. You feel more shaky.
  • If they ask for ipratropium or prednisolone, the nurse gives it. Nothing changes within the station time.
  • If they call the senior ED doctor, the nurse says, "They're on their way, keep going."
  • If they do nothing for your breathing in the first few minutes, the nurse says, "Her sats are 90% on room air and her resp rate is 36," and you can only manage one or two words at a time.
  • If they ask you to lie back, you say, "I can't... I need to sit up."
  • If they ask for a peak flow, the examiner says she is too breathless to do a reliable blow at the moment.
  • If they explain calmly what they are doing, you settle a little. If they use jargon, look confused.
  • If they ask for results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I feel like... I'm gasping... for air."

History (give only when asked; a few words at a time):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: sudden, about an hour ago, while you were jogging outside.
  • Course: it got worse as you kept jogging. It has kept getting worse, and the ambulance neb helped only a bit.
  • Character: "Like I'm gasping for air." Your chest feels tight.
  • Severity: you had to stop and sit on the footpath. A passer-by called the ambulance.
  • Reliever: you forgot to take your Ventolin before you went jogging and did not have it with you.

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Wheeze: yes, you can hear yourself wheezing.
  • Cough: a dry cough that has been worse at night since a cold about 2 weeks ago. No phlegm.
  • Heart: your heart is racing. It feels fast but regular, and it started with the breathlessness. It has been worse and your hands shakier since the ambulance treatment. No fainting.
  • Recent illness: a cold about 2 weeks ago, now gone apart from the cough. No fever, sweats or shivers now.

Questions about the other causes (all no, only if asked)

  • Clots: no pain or swelling in either calf. No sharp pain on breathing in, no coughing up blood. No long trips, operations or time laid up in bed. You have never had a clot, and nobody in your family has.
  • Collapsed lung: no fall or knock to the chest, no one-sided sharp pain, never had a collapsed lung.
  • Chest infection: no fever, no coloured phlegm.
  • Choking: you were not eating or drinking anything, and nothing went down the wrong way.
  • Allergic reaction: no swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, no tingling in the mouth, no hoarse voice, no hives or rash, no tummy pain, vomiting or diarrhoea. You feel a bit light-headed only from the breathing, not faint. You had not eaten anything new.
  • Anxiety: you have never had panic attacks. You are anxious now because you cannot breathe.

Triggers (only if asked)

  • Exercise: you have just started jogging.
  • The cold 2 weeks ago.
  • Your boyfriend smokes.
  • Dust sets you off.
  • Your family got a new puppy recently.

Past medical history

  • Asthma, diagnosed at 18. Your GP manages it.
  • Only if asked: you have never been admitted to hospital or ICU for asthma, never needed a breathing tube, and never had a course of prednisolone (steroid tablets).
  • Only if asked about control: before the cold you hardly used your Ventolin. Since the cold you have been using it a few times a week, mainly for the night cough. You do not have a preventer inhaler or a written asthma action plan.
  • Eczema, in the creases of your elbows.

Medications

  • Ventolin (salbutamol) puffer when needed. You use it without a spacer.
  • Telfast (fexofenadine) for hay fever.
  • The combined oral contraceptive pill.
  • Nothing else, no supplements.

Allergies: hay fever. No medicine allergies.

Family history: your brother has asthma and eczema. Your mother is well. Your father has type 1 diabetes.

Social history

  • Never smoked. You do not drink alcohol. No recreational drugs.
  • Law student.
  • You have been very sedentary and only just started jogging.
  • You live with your parents and brother. You are well supported.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: at first you thought you were just unfit because you had only just started jogging. "I'm really anxious because I can't breathe and my heart's racing." You want to be able to breathe and you want someone to call your mum.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "Is my heart OK? It's going so fast."

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: young woman sitting upright and leaning forward, anxious, in obvious respiratory distress. Using her neck muscles to breathe. Speaking 3 or 4 words at a time. Audible wheeze. Alert and not exhausted. Not cyanosed. Fine tremor of both hands.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill under 2 seconds. No clubbing.
  • Pulse: 126/min, regular, good volume.
  • Blood pressure: 128/76.
  • Face, mouth and neck: no swelling of the lips, tongue or face. No stridor. Voice normal apart from breathlessness. Trachea central.
  • Skin: dry, scaly eczema in both elbow creases. No hives or rash.
  • Chest inspection and palpation: chest looks hyperinflated. Expansion reduced but equal on both sides. Chest wall not tender, no bruising.
  • Percussion: resonant throughout and the same on both sides.
  • Auscultation: widespread high-pitched expiratory wheeze over both lungs, with a prolonged expiratory phase. Air entry is reduced but present and equal on both sides. Not a silent chest. No crackles, no bronchial breathing, no pleural rub.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, tachycardic, no murmurs.
  • Legs: calves soft and non-tender, no swelling.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Sophia's identity and asks whether she is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Recognises a severe attack from the nurse's observations and her speech, and starts treatment before taking a detailed history: keeps her sitting upright, asks for oxygen with a stated target, asks for inhaled salbutamol and calls the senior ED doctor.
check.d: Credit when a bronchodilator and oxygen are requested within the first few minutes and senior help is called. No credit for high-flow oxygen without a target.

check.x: Acknowledges her fear calmly and keeps questions short and mostly closed so she can answer in a few words.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when onset and at least 2 of the other 3 are elicited.

kids.x: Onset: sudden, an hour ago, while jogging outside
Course: worse as she kept jogging and still getting worse; the paramedics' nebuliser helped only a little
Reliever: forgot to take her Ventolin before jogging and did not have it with her

check.x: Elicits the associated asthma symptoms: chest tightness, wheeze, and a dry cough worse at night.
Asks about triggers: exercise, the cold 2 weeks ago, her boyfriend's smoking, dust and the new puppy.
check.d: Credit when at least 3 triggers are elicited.

check.x: Asks about markers of severe or high-risk asthma: previous hospital and ICU admissions, intubation and courses of oral prednisolone (none), plus current control (more reliever use and night cough since the cold, no preventer, no action plan).
check.d: Credit when hospital or ICU admission and systemic steroid use are both asked about.

check.x: Takes the medication and allergy history: Ventolin as needed without a spacer, Telfast, the combined oral contraceptive pill; hay fever, no medicine allergies.
Screens for the other causes of acute dyspnoea:
check.d: Credit when at least 4 differentials are screened with relevant questions, which must include PE (with the combined pill noted) and anaphylaxis.

kids.x: PE: calf pain or swelling, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility, previous or family VTE; notes the combined pill
Pneumothorax: chest trauma, one-sided pleuritic pain, previous pneumothorax
Anaphylaxis: lip, tongue or throat swelling, tingling mouth, hoarse voice, hives, dizziness, GI symptoms
Aspiration or inhaled foreign body: choking
Arrhythmia: character of the racing heart (regular, began with the breathlessness), syncope
Anxiety or hyperventilation: previous panic attacks

check.x: Past history of asthma (diagnosed at 18, GP-managed) and eczema; family history of asthma and atopy (brother).
Asks about smoking (never) and second-hand smoke exposure (boyfriend smokes), and who is with her or can be contacted (lives with parents; wants mum called).
check.d: Credit when smoking is asked about.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thought she was just unfit, anxious because she cannot breathe and her heart is racing, wants to breathe and wants her mum called.
Examination

Assesses severity on general inspection: words per breath (3 to 4), accessory muscle use, posture, cyanosis (none), conscious state and exhaustion (alert, not tiring), audible wheeze, tremor, and the nurse's observations.
check.d: Credit when words per breath, accessory muscle use and conscious state/exhaustion are all assessed.

check.x: Respiratory examination:
check.d: Credit when percussion and auscultation are both performed and compared side to side.

kids.x: Trachea central; chest hyperinflated with reduced but equal expansion
Resonant and symmetrical on percussion (no one-sided hyper-resonance)
Widespread bilateral expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiration, equal air entry, not a silent chest, no crackles

check.x: Looks for anaphylaxis (lip, tongue or facial swelling, stridor, hives: all absent) and notes the flexural eczema.
Examines the pulse (regular), heart sounds and calves (soft, non-tender, no swelling, against DVT).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR 32 to 34 is in the red zone, calling for a rapid response (senior ED doctor at the bedside now); SpO2 92% on room air and HR 126 are yellow zone; BP and temperature are normal.
check.d: Credit when the red-zone RR is identified with immediate escalation.

check.x: Interprets the arterial blood gas:
check.d: Credit when acute respiratory alkalosis without renal compensation is stated (source marking).

kids.x: HCO3 22: no renal (metabolic) compensation, consistent with the expected acute buffering fall, so the process is acute
States that a low pCO2 is expected early in acute asthma, that a normal or rising pCO2 would mean she is tiring (life-threatening), and that pO2 132 was measured on supplemental oxygen

check.x: Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia (salbutamol, distress, hypoxia) with no arrhythmia and no right heart strain, and states that this does not exclude PE.

Classifies the attack as severe acute asthma (Australian Asthma Handbook): cannot complete sentences in one breath, accessory muscle use, obvious distress, SpO2 90 to 94%. States it is not life-threatening: alert, not cyanosed, SpO2 not below 90%, wheeze audible, pCO2 low.
check.d: Credit when graded severe with at least 2 severe features and stated not life-threatening with at least 1 reason.

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as an acute exacerbation of asthma, justified by known asthma, an exercise trigger without her pre-exercise reliever, a recent viral infection and allergen exposure, wheeze, chest tightness and night cough, atopy and family history, plus relevant negatives.

Names differentials, each with a feature from this patient: PE (combined pill and sudden onset, but wheeze, no pleuritic pain, calves normal), anaphylaxis (sudden wheeze during exercise in an atopic woman, but no angioedema, hives or hypotension), pneumothorax (symmetrical signs), anxiety or hyperventilation (only once organic causes are excluded).
check.d: Credit when at least 3 differentials are named, each with a feature for or against.

check.x: Management
Escalates: senior ED doctor at the bedside, resus or acute bay with continuous cardiac and SpO2 monitoring, frequent observations.
Restarts oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95% (Australian Asthma Handbook), as she is 92% on room air. Oxygen is titrated to target, not given at high flow without a target.

Gives salbutamol 12 puffs (100 microgram each) by pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or salbutamol 5 mg by oxygen-driven nebuliser every 20 minutes for the first hour if she cannot use a spacer.
Adds ipratropium for severe asthma: 8 puffs (21 microgram each) by pMDI and spacer, or a 500 microgram nebule, every 20 minutes for the first hour.
Gives a systemic corticosteroid within the first hour: prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly if she cannot take tablets), continued for 5 to 10 days.

Plans reassessment and escalation if she does not respond: IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes, repeat gas if she tires or SpO2 falls (rising pCO2), early ICU review. Chest X-ray only if pneumothorax or consolidation is suspected or she fails to respond. Reconsiders PE if she does not improve as expected. Admits her if she still needs frequent bronchodilator after the first hour.
check.d: Credit when IV magnesium and ICU involvement are both named as the next steps.

check.x: Safety netting

Explains in plain words that her airways narrowed and became inflamed, set off by jogging on top of her recent cold; answers her questions (she can keep jogging once controlled, taking her reliever beforehand). Checks understanding.

Tells Sophia to seek urgent review if she needs her reliever again within 3 hours, and to call 000 if the reliever is not helping, she cannot speak in sentences, her lips turn blue or she is drowsy; outlines asthma first aid (4 puffs by spacer, wait 4 minutes, repeat, then 000).
check.d: Credit when the reliever-within-3-hours rule and at least 2 specific reasons to call 000 (reliever not helping, cannot speak in sentences, blue lips, drowsy) are given; first-aid steps are a bonus.

check.x: Arranges discharge treatment: an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer, a written asthma action plan and GP review within a week.
check.d: Credit when the preventer and the action plan are named. Bonus, not scored: completing the prednisolone course, checking spacer technique, trigger advice (reliever 5 to 20 minutes before exercise; avoid smoke).

part2.lead: Here are her observations, the arterial blood gas taken on arrival and the ECG the nurse recorded.
part2.patient:
Ask this only after the examiner reads question 4, still a little breathless:

  • "Is this because I forgot my Ventolin? Can I still go jogging?"

You are relieved there is a plan. If the candidate explains clearly, you agree to it and say you would like someone to show you the spacer before you go. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: The 14:22 set was taken on arrival while the paramedics' salbutamol nebuliser was running through a nebuliser mask on oxygen 8 L/min. The 14:32 set was taken on room air after the nebuliser finished, before the medical review.
handover.model:
• Read: on arrival, RR 34 (red zone), SpO2 98% on the oxygen-driven nebuliser, HR 130 (yellow zone), BP 130/80. On room air at 14:32: RR 32 (red), SpO2 92% (yellow), HR 126 (yellow), BP 128/76, temperature 37.2 °C (white), alert. She is still severely distressed after a prehospital nebuliser.
  • Meaning: severe respiratory distress with hypoxaemia on room air and tachycardia (from the attack and the salbutamol). The normal BP and alert state show she is not peri-arrest. She is afebrile.
  • Changes: the red-zone RR calls for a rapid response, which in the ED means the senior doctor at the bedside now. Restart oxygen titrated to 93 to 95%, give repeated bronchodilators, and repeat observations at least every 15 minutes.

rows.note: Arrived by ambulance; paramedic salbutamol neb running via nebuliser mask on 8 L/min O2; arterial gas taken
Neb finished; mask off for room-air set before medical review; pain 3 = chest tightness

handover.label: Arterial blood gas
handover.result: Arterial sample, right radial, collected 14:22 on arrival while a salbutamol nebuliser was running on oxygen 8 L/min. Patient temperature 37.2 °C.
handover.model:
• Read: pH 7.51, so alkalaemia. pCO2 28 mmHg is low, so the cause is respiratory. HCO3 22: no renal (metabolic) compensation, consistent with the expected acute buffering fall, so the process is acute. The base excess is normal, so there is no primary metabolic process. pO2 132 mmHg (SaO2 99%) was measured on supplemental oxygen, so she is well oxygenated on it, and cannot be compared with the room-air range. Potassium and lactate are normal now; recheck them during repeated salbutamol.
  • Meaning: acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, driven by bronchospasm, hypoxaemia and anxiety. This is expected early in acute asthma and is reassuring because she is not tiring. A normal or rising pCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is a life-threatening sign. The gas does not separate asthma from PE or hyperventilation; the clinical picture does.
  • Changes: restart oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95% (she is 92% on room air); avoid high-flow oxygen without a target. A repeat gas is needed only if she tires, becomes drowsy or her SpO2 falls.

labs.title: Arterial blood gas (14:22, on oxygen 8 L/min via nebuliser)

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Ms Sophia Bennett, age 20, recorded at 14:25 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 128/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia. Regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +70°.
  • PR interval: 140 ms. No delta wave.
  • QRS duration: 84 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 430 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression. T waves upright except in aVR and V1.
  • Other: no S1Q3T3 pattern, no right axis deviation, no P pulmonale. Normal R wave progression.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
  • Conclusion: sinus tachycardia, otherwise normal ECG.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 128/min. Normal axis, PR, QRS and QTc. No pre-excitation, no ST or T wave change, and no signs of right heart strain.
  • Meaning: her racing heart is a sinus tachycardia from distress, hypoxaemia and salbutamol, not an SVT or other arrhythmia. There is no right heart strain, but a normal ECG does not exclude PE.
  • Changes: no arrhythmia treatment is needed. Keep her on the monitor during repeated salbutamol, and reconsider PE if she does not improve with asthma treatment.

ask: You are calling the medical registrar to let them know about Sophia, who is likely to need admission. Please give an ISBAR handover, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and how severe is it? What else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sophia now, here in the emergency department.
Sophia improves and is later ready to go home. Before she goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student in ED; Sophia Bennett, 20.
  • Situation: severe acute asthma; RR 32 (red zone), SpO2 92% on room air, HR 126 after a paramedic salbutamol nebuliser.
  • Background: sudden breathlessness an hour ago while jogging, without her pre-exercise Ventolin; wheeze, tightness and night cough since a cold 2 weeks ago; asthma since 18, reliever only, never admitted, never on prednisolone; atopic; on the combined pill; no medicine allergies.
  • Assessment: speaks 3 to 4 words, uses accessory muscles, widespread wheeze, equal air entry, no anaphylaxis signs. ABG on oxygen: acute respiratory alkalosis without compensation, pCO2 28, so not tiring. ECG: sinus tachycardia.
  • Recommendation: treatment started: oxygen to 93 to 95%, salbutamol and ipratropium every 20 minutes, prednisolone given. Please review her for admission; I will escalate to ICU if she tires or her pCO2 rises.

Severity (Australian Asthma Handbook): severe: speaks 3 to 4 words per breath, uses accessory muscles, obvious distress, SpO2 92% on room air. Not life-threatening: alert, not exhausted or cyanosed, SpO2 not below 90%, wheeze audible (not a silent chest), pCO2 28 (not above 50).

Severe acute exacerbation of asthma: known asthma, exercise trigger without her reliever, recent viral infection, allergens (puppy, dust, smoke); wheeze, tightness, night cough; atopy and family history; widespread bilateral wheeze; low pCO2.

  • PE: for: combined pill, sudden onset, tachycardia, hypoxaemia, respiratory alkalosis; against: wheeze, no pleuritic pain or haemoptysis, calves normal.
  • Anaphylaxis: for: sudden wheeze during exercise in an atopic woman; against: no angioedema, stridor, hives, GI symptoms or hypotension.
  • Pneumothorax: for: asthma, exertion; against: no pleuritic pain, symmetrical resonance and air entry.
  • Optional: Anxiety or hyperventilation: for: low pCO2, racing heart; against: wheeze and hypoxaemia. Diagnose only once organic causes are excluded.

1. Senior ED doctor at the bedside; continuous monitoring; sit her upright.
  2. Oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95%.
  3. Salbutamol 12 puffs (100 microgram each) by pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or salbutamol 5 mg by oxygen-driven nebuliser every 20 minutes for the first hour if she cannot use a spacer.
  4. Ipratropium 8 puffs (or 500 microgram nebule) every 20 minutes for the first hour.
  5. Prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally within the first hour (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if she cannot take tablets).
  6. Reassess often; recheck potassium and lactate during repeated salbutamol. If she does not respond: IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes, repeat gas, ICU review. Chest X-ray only if pneumothorax is suspected or she fails to respond; reconsider PE. Admit if she still needs frequent bronchodilator after the first hour.

• Explanation: her airways narrowed and became inflamed, set off by jogging on top of her recent cold; forgetting the reliever made it worse. Her questions: she can keep jogging once her asthma is controlled, taking her reliever beforehand. Checks understanding.
  • Red flags: reliever needed again within 3 hours: seek urgent review. Call 000 if the reliever is not helping, she cannot speak in sentences, her lips turn blue or she is drowsy. First aid: 4 puffs by spacer, wait 4 minutes, repeat, then 000.
  • Medicines and follow-up: preventer containing an inhaled steroid, finish prednisolone, spacer technique, written action plan; GP within a week.
  • Triggers: reliever before exercise, avoid cigarette smoke.

ddx.for: Known asthma, sudden breathlessness while jogging without her pre-exercise reliever, a recent cold, allergen and smoke exposure, wheeze, chest tightness and night cough, atopy, widespread bilateral wheeze and a low pCO2.
She takes the combined pill and has sudden breathlessness with tachycardia, hypoxaemia on room air and a respiratory alkalosis.
ddx.against: Widespread wheeze with an asthma trigger, no pleuritic pain or haemoptysis, no immobility or previous clot, and soft, non-tender calves.

ddx.for: Sudden wheeze during exercise in an atopic woman.
ddx.against: No lip, tongue or throat swelling, no stridor, hives or GI symptoms, and a normal BP.

ddx.for: Sudden breathlessness during exertion in a patient with asthma.
ddx.against: No pleuritic or one-sided pain, no trauma, a central trachea, and symmetrical resonance and air entry.

ddx.for: She is very anxious with a racing heart and a pCO2 of 28 mmHg.
ddx.against: No history of panic attacks, audible widespread wheeze and an SpO2 of 92% on room air show an organic cause.

ddx.dx: Viral lower respiratory tract infection or pneumonia
ddx.for: A cold 2 weeks ago with a lingering cough.
ddx.against: Dry cough, no fever, sputum or focal crackles, and a temperature of 37.2 °C.

guide:
In Part 1, the nurse gives the arrival and room-air observations at the start. Sophia answers in a few words at a time. A good candidate acts on the severity first (sits her up, gives oxygen with a target and salbutamol, calls the senior doctor) and then takes a targeted history; this earns item 3. Give the improvement described in the script only if a bronchodilator and oxygen are ordered. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Sophia mentions the night cough, the triggers and her steroid and admission history only if asked. If the candidate asks for results in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Sophia asks her question after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate starts treatment within the first minutes, asks about previous ICU and hospital admissions and prednisolone courses, and screens PE (noting the pill), anaphylaxis and pneumothorax with targeted questions. They examine for severity and compare the two sides of the chest. In Part 2 they read the gas as an acute respiratory alkalosis without compensation and explain why a low pCO2 is expected and a normal one would be ominous. They grade the attack as severe and treat it with correctly dosed salbutamol, ipratropium and prednisolone, with magnesium and ICU as the next steps. They send her home on a preventer with an action plan.

A borderline candidate takes a full history before treating, does not ask about previous severe attacks or steroid use, misses the pill, or calls the gas "normal oxygenation" without commenting on the pCO2. Labelling her breathlessness as anxiety, delaying bronchodilators, or discharging her on a reliever alone without an action plan is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: severe acute exacerbation of asthma

Sophia has known asthma that has been poorly controlled since a cold 2 weeks ago. She takes a reliever only and has no preventer, and her night cough and rising reliever use show this. She became suddenly breathless while jogging, having forgotten to take her Ventolin beforehand, and kept running as it got worse. Exercise, a recent viral infection, dust, cigarette smoke and a new pet are all classic triggers. Her eczema, hay fever and a brother with asthma and eczema complete an atopic picture.

Assess severity and treat first

In acute dyspnoea, think first of the life-threatening causes: myocardial infarction, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, PE, acute asthma, aspiration and anaphylaxis. When asthma is suspected, take a brief history and assess severity, then start oxygen and bronchodilators before taking a detailed history. The Australian Asthma Handbook grades acute asthma in adults:

  • Mild to moderate: can walk and speak whole sentences in one breath.
  • Severe: any of: accessory muscle use, tracheal tug or recession; cannot complete sentences in one breath; obvious respiratory distress; SpO2 90 to 94%.
  • Life-threatening: any of: reduced consciousness, collapse, exhaustion, cyanosis, SpO2 below 90%, PaCO2 above 50 mmHg, poor respiratory effort, soft or absent breath sounds (silent chest).

Sophia has severe asthma: she speaks 3 to 4 words at a time, uses her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 92% on room air. She has no life-threatening features. Do not delay treatment to get a peak flow from a patient this breathless.

The history

  • Risk of a fatal attack: ask about previous ICU admission or intubation, hospital admissions, systemic corticosteroid courses, poor control, high reliever use, and no preventer. Sophia has never been admitted or had prednisolone, but she has no preventer and her control is getting worse.
  • Differentials: PE (calf swelling, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, oestrogen, immobility, previous or family VTE), pneumothorax (trauma, pleuritic pain, previous episode), pneumonia, aspiration (choking), anaphylaxis (angioedema, tingling mouth, hoarse voice, hives, dizziness, GI symptoms), pleural effusion, arrhythmia and anxiety. Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion; a frightened, breathless patient with wheeze has an organic cause until proven otherwise.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: a red-zone RR calls for a rapid response; yellow-zone SpO2 and HR call for clinical review. She is still distressed after a prehospital nebuliser.
  • Arterial gas: pH high (alkalaemia), pCO2 low (respiratory), HCO3 22: no renal (metabolic) compensation, consistent with the expected acute buffering fall (about 2 mmol/L per 10 mmHg fall in pCO2), so the process is acute: an acute respiratory alkalosis. Early in acute asthma, hyperventilation drives the pCO2 down. As the patient tires, the pCO2 rises back to "normal" and then above it. A normal or high pCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is a life-threatening sign that needs ICU. Her pO2 of 132 mmHg was measured on oxygen, so it says only that she oxygenates well on oxygen; give oxygen titrated to 93 to 95% rather than high flow without a target. A blood gas is not needed in every patient with acute asthma; repeat it if she tires, becomes drowsy or desaturates.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia is expected with distress, hypoxaemia and salbutamol. It excludes an arrhythmia as the cause of her racing heart, but a normal ECG does not exclude PE.
  • Chest X-ray is not routinely needed in acute asthma. Request it if pneumothorax, consolidation or another diagnosis is suspected, or if she does not respond to treatment.

Management (Australian Asthma Handbook: acute asthma in adults)

  1. Escalate and monitor: senior doctor at the bedside, continuous monitoring, sit her upright.
  2. Oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95%.
  3. Salbutamol: for severe asthma, 12 puffs (100 microgram each) by pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or salbutamol 5 mg by oxygen-driven nebuliser every 20 minutes for the first hour if she cannot use a spacer. Life-threatening asthma needs continuous nebulised salbutamol.
  4. Ipratropium for severe or life-threatening asthma: 8 puffs (21 microgram each) by spacer, or a 500 microgram nebule, every 20 minutes for the first hour.
  5. Systemic corticosteroid within the first hour: prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally, or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly if oral is not possible, continued for 5 to 10 days.
  6. If she does not respond: IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes, a repeat gas and an ICU review for possible IV bronchodilators or ventilation. Sedatives are contraindicated. Watch for salbutamol side effects: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia and a raised lactate. If she improves less than expected, think again about PE (she is on the combined pill) and pneumothorax.
  7. Disposition: admit if she still needs frequent bronchodilator after the first hour of treatment. Consider discharge only after a sustained response on room air, with senior review.

Discharge and safety netting

Every adult discharged after acute asthma needs an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer (for example budesonide-formoterol). She also needs to finish the prednisolone course, have her spacer technique checked and leave with a written asthma action plan. Teach asthma first aid (National Asthma Council): sit upright, give 4 separate puffs of the reliever through a spacer with 4 breaths each, wait 4 minutes and repeat, and call 000 if there is no improvement. She should call 000 if her reliever is not helping, she cannot finish sentences, her lips turn blue or she becomes drowsy. Advise using her reliever (salbutamol, or budesonide-formoterol if that is her prescribed reliever) 5 to 20 minutes before exercise and warming up, keeping away from cigarette smoke (her boyfriend should not smoke near her), and asking her GP about allergy assessment for the puppy and dust. She should have a yearly influenza vaccine. Arrange GP review within a week, with a discharge summary, to review her control and step up treatment.
points: In acute breathlessness with wheeze, assess severity from speech, accessory muscle use, conscious state and SpO2, and start oxygen and bronchodilators before taking a detailed history.
In known asthma, always ask about previous ICU admission or intubation, hospital admissions and courses of systemic corticosteroids, and about current control and preventer use.
Early in acute asthma, hyperventilation gives a respiratory alkalosis with a low pCO2. A normal or rising pCO2 in a breathless asthmatic means exhaustion and life-threatening asthma.
Interpret a pO2 against the oxygen the patient was breathing, and give oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95% in acute asthma rather than high flow without a target.

Severe acute asthma: salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer and ipratropium 8 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour, prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg within the hour, then IV magnesium and ICU review if she does not respond.

Screen PE, anaphylaxis and pneumothorax in every young adult with sudden dyspnoea (note oestrogen use), and discharge after acute asthma only on an inhaled steroid preventer with an action plan, asthma first aid and GP review within a week.
